name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47

voice.register: Fast, warm and run-on: a man walking between two building sites with his right arm up, talking to someone far away. His shape is the one run-on that grows: clauses chained with commas, 'aur haan' and 'aur ek', and no full stop till the last bubble, so a long thought takes two to four bubbles of at most ten words, each ending on a comma until the last ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, aur haan,' / 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao, chairs bhi,' / 'sabko andar lo, sabko jagah. Pakka?'). It is the longest single sentence in the cast and it is told apart from the other long runs by its ending: Papa's are whole sentences with full stops, Masterji's a verdict and a wander, Mausi's a tripled word and a question she answers herself, and his is one sentence that never quite ends. His questions are worry checks about named people, stacked, and he waits only for the answer to the last one, 'Pakka?'; he never answers them himself. Feeling is said out loud, warmly, to one person at a time, with a hug: he is one of the two elders who say it in plain words (Mausi says hers to the whole room, loud; he says his to one face). Fear he says only to Mami. Humour is big and kind and aimed at himself (he plans nothing, he talks too much), never at anyone's age, town, shop or work. He talks most to people far away, Mummy first ('Didi!'); in chapter 5, with the phone in his pocket, to everyone at the gate. With Nani alone he slows to short whole sentences, the only person he slows for, and lets her finish before he speaks. When cross he does not go quiet or slow (that is Mami's tell in his chapter): the run-on stops dead and breaks into single words, one downward chop of his free hand on each ('Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.'), and even then he asks after the other man's family first. Never at family, a woman, a worker's dignity or anyone on a card. His voice is never raised except the chapter's one shout at 5.03 (rule 35). Warm, and never the comic one while he is the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: The most English elder. Hinglish: a whole English clause first, at speed, then a Hindi landing ('Don't worry, Bade Jija ji ko bulao, aur haan,'). The order and the cargo are his alone: his English leads and carries the jobs and the warmth (don't worry, no problem, sorted, extra, full, credit, department, I missed you, I'll miss you), and his Hindi lands on family, food and feeling (Amma, Didi, ghar, sab, khaana, dawai, man, roz). Mami, the other whole-clause switcher, runs the other way: a Hindi clause, then an English status ('pending', 'done', 'Correct?'). He never builds an English verb with kar or ho ('check karo', 'confirm karo', 'call karo'), because that frame is Mummy's alone: his English comes as whole clauses or bare nouns ('ticket bhi book?'). 'Ek kaam karo' to you, Tinku and Mami; 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders. Figures in Hinglish bubbles are digits ('60? 70 kar do!'), because romanised 'saath' is also 'with' (India review). HINDI MODE: everyday spoken city Hindi in Devanagari that keeps more English loan words than anyone else's (एक्स्ट्रा, फ़ुल, सेट, नो प्रॉब्लम, क्रेडिट, डिपार्टमेंट, प्रमोशन), so he still sorts in Hindi; 'चिंता मत करो' or 'चिंता नहीं' for 'don't worry' (never फ़िक्र, Masterji's word); with Nani, whole Hindi sentences and आप. ENGLISH MODE: plain British English with his rhythm, the trailing comma and 'oh, and' for 'aur haan'; 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter (his one Indian-English turn), otherwise 'One small job'; 'Oho!' stays; kin words stay as they are (Didi, Jija ji, Amma, Boss); never a spelled accent (caricature traps). With Nani in English mode the slowing carries the beat that Hindi mode carries with whole Hindi sentences.
tics: The run-on that grows: 'Ek kaam karo,' and the one thing grows ('aur haan,', 'aur ek,') until it is four; every bubble but the last ends on a comma. In English mode 'aur haan' is 'oh, and'.

Stacks worry questions about named people and waits only for the last answer: 'Amma ka BP? Dawai? Koi saath hai? Pakka?'. He never answers his own question (Mausi's shape) and never asks how you are (Nani's 'Aur tum.' closes that in the album).
Ends every worry stack and every reassurance he is given with 'Pakka?' ('Sure?'); at 5.27 it turns round into a statement.

People first, then business: every vendor gets 'Ghar mein sab theek?' and a question about their own people (a mother's knee, the children's exams) before 'Achha,' and the job. Names, not numbers, are his stock, and he keeps it even when cross.

Makes everything bigger in words, never in figures: aur, sab, sabko, extra, full ('full family', 'full kasoor', 'full fit'). The plus-ten is a gesture, the flashed open hand, with no figure said; the only spoken figures in his year are 5.03 and 5.27.
Hands the how to someone else in the same breath: 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao,', 'Credit Jija ji ka,'. He plans nothing; he knows who can.

Credits people out loud by their job, to whoever is near: 'In-charge se miliye!', 'Ghar ki railway se miliye!', and from December 'District scorer se miliye!' (outside any decision beat, guests off the panel).
'Oho!' for good or bad news, by tone; 'Achha,' as the hinge from the family question to the job; 'Aaiye' once at the gate, never three times (triples are Mausi's).
Never talks over Nani: he lets her finish, then repeats her last two words back.
Hugs everyone he can reach while he says it out loud (a stage direction, never a word). Never you: household hands never reach towards you (rule 7).
catchphrases: 'Ek kaam karo, ... aur haan,' | 'एक काम करो, ... और हाँ,' | 'Do one thing, ... oh, and,' The one thing that becomes four. 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders; in English mode 'Do one thing' once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job,'. The 'ek' is an idiom, not a count.
'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?' The end of every worry stack, his word in the cast table. Turned round once, at 5.27: 'Pakka.' | 'पक्का।' | 'For sure.'

'60? 70 kar do!' | 'साठ? सत्तर कर दो!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!' His quoted line and his only catchphrase with a number, said once, at 5.03, the chapter's one shout, with the open hand flashed. The owner is asked whether to keep both marked figures (matrix open point).
voice.exclamation: 'Oho!' | 'ओहो!' | 'Oho!' (the same in every mode). For good news and bad, and the tone tells which: a rising 'Oho!' with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at a delay. It is a sound with no word in it, so it has no religious sense, and it is his alone in the cast (the India review and Mami's file both give it to him). Guard: never run on into a god-word, and never the city man's reflexes 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Shukar hai' or 'Bhagwan ka shukar' (rule 3). Never 'Kamaal!' (Papa's 'Kamaal hai.') and never any 'arre' (Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.').
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: blame, out loud and made bigger, the way he makes everything bigger: 'Didi, full kasoor mera. Full!' | 'दीदी, पूरा क़सूर मेरा। पूरा!' | 'Didi, it's all my fault. All of it!'. Said to whoever he let down, Mummy most of all, in front of everyone, and never with the English word 'sorry' (Mausi's alone). THANKS: public credit by job, loudly, to whoever is near, so the thank-you is the room hearing what you did: 'In-charge se miliye!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the in-charge!'; for Papa 'Ghar ki railway se miliye!' | 'घर की रेलवे से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the family's railway!'. Thanked himself, he gives the credit away to whoever did the how: 'Not me! Credit Jija ji ka.' He never says 'thank you' or 'shukriya' (Mami's to strangers, and yours). LOVE: said in plain words, one to one, with a hug: 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगा। रोज़।' | 'Amma, I missed you. Every day.'; at a parting 'Didi, I'll miss you.' | 'दीदी, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगेगा।' and the worry stack after it; to Mami in private, what she did, said back to her ('aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha.'). Never 'bahut yaad' or 'याद आई' (Mausi's). FEAR: only to Mami ('Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.').
uses: 'Ek kaam karo' | 'एक काम करो' | 'Do one thing' (to vendors and elders 'Ek kaam kijiye' | 'एक काम कीजिए')
'aur haan' / 'aur ek' | 'और हाँ' / 'और एक' | 'oh, and' / 'one more', always trailing into the next bubble
'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?'
'Don't worry' | 'चिंता मत करो' / 'चिंता नहीं' | 'Don't worry' (to others, never about himself; Mummy's, Papa's and Mausa ji's files already name it his)
'No problem' | 'नो प्रॉब्लम' | 'No problem' (comfort)
'Achha,' | 'अच्छा,' | 'Right,' or 'Good,' (the hinge from people to the job; Mami's file names it his)
'sorted' | 'सेट' | 'sorted' (the word he wants back from you)
'full' before people, blame and health: 'full family', 'full kasoor', 'full fit' | 'फ़ुल' / 'पूरा' | 'whole', 'all', 'fighting fit'
'extra' | 'एक्स्ट्रा' | 'extra'
'sab', 'sabko', 'aur' as his bigger numbers | 'सब', 'सबको', 'और' | 'everyone', 'more'
'Ghar mein sab theek?' | 'घर में सब ठीक?' | 'All well at home?' (to every vendor, before business)
'Maa ji ka ghutna?', 'Bachchon ke exam?' | 'माँ जी का घुटना?', 'बच्चों के इम्तिहान?' | 'Your mother's knee?', 'The children's exams?' (his phone book, by family)
'credit' | 'क्रेडिट' | 'credit' (always given away)
'[job] se miliye!' | '[जॉब] से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the [job]!'
'department' | 'डिपार्टमेंट' | 'department' (his joke at himself: plans are Boss's department)
'arrangement' | 'इंतज़ाम' | 'arrangements'; 'last minute' | 'ऐन वक़्त पर' | 'at the last minute'; 'advance' | 'एडवांस' | 'advance' (5.06)
'Roz' | 'रोज़' | 'Every day' (his love word, after 'I missed you')
'man nahi laga' | 'मन नहीं लगा' | 'I missed you' (his Hindi for it)
'Aaiye' | 'आइए' | 'Come in' (guests, once)
'Oho' | 'ओहो' | 'Oho'
Trade words, only outside chapter 5: pressure, flow, site, order, dispatch, pump.
never: Any spoken figure but the two marked beats (5.03 '60? 70 kar do!', 5.27 '60 plates. Pakka.'): no counts, times, prices, ages, 'do din', '60 kursiyaan'; no ordinals, not even 'first job' or 'first class'. The idiom 'ek kaam' is not a count.
A number smaller than his last, or 'kam karo' | 'कम करो' | 'cut it', in public. The one exception is 5.27.
'Nahi' to a guest; 'pata nahi' | 'पता नहीं' | 'I don't know'; 'baad mein dekhenge' | 'बाद में देखेंगे' | 'we'll see later'.
An English verb built with kar or ho ('check karo', 'confirm karo', 'book karo', 'call karo', 'arrange ho jayega'): that frame is Mummy's alone.

Other people's words (matrix 2.15, one owner each): 'sorry', 'tension', 'first class', 'Haaye', 'Suno', 'hai na?', 'bahut yaad' and a bare 'Bahut' (Mausi); 'Kamaal', 'Noted', a bare 'Reached?', a time to the minute (Papa); 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' as one-word lines, 'Galti hui', 'Ho jayega', 'Mazboot', 'Hain?' (Mausa ji); 'Bas', 'Chai piyo', 'Baap re', 'poori gali' (Nani); 'hisaab', 'Iska bill nahin', 'Had hai' (Mummy); 'Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well fielded', any 'arre' (Captain sahab); 'Correct?', 'pending', 'done', 'Tick', 'Ish' (Mami); 'fikr', 'Uff', 'Dekhiye' as an opener (Masterji); 'Gazab', 'Mera wicket', 'Run tumhara' (Tinku); 'Pehle ___', 'Shukriya', 'Maaf kijiye', 'Badhiya' (yours); 'sharp' (three askers wore it out).

Other people's shapes: answering his own question or tripling a word (Mausi); the number before the noun (Papa, Tinku); items as 'thing, status' (Mami); closed fragments outside his cross beat (Nani); tea as his care (Nani's sorry, Masterji's love).
'Thank you' or 'thanks' to anyone: his thank-you is credit given away out loud.

Religious words and exclamations (rule 3): 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Hai Ram', 'Bhagwan', 'Shukar hai', 'Inshallah', 'Mashallah', 'Rab', 'Wahe Guru', 'Jesus'; in English mode also 'Gosh', 'Good Lord', 'Thank goodness', 'Thank heavens', 'Heavens'.
Famous titles that pass for everyday phrases (rule 3): 'Main hoon na', 'Badhaai ho'.
Dowry or ritual words: 'dahej' | 'दहेज', 'lena-dena' | 'लेन-देन', 'kanyadaan', 'vidaai', 'phere', 'mandap', 'shagun', 'baraat'; nothing at all about gifts for the groom's side (rules 22 and 27).
His daughter's name or looks, or 'giving her away'.
'Chhota shehar' | 'छोटा शहर' | 'small town', or any put-down of Nani's town, Mummy's shop or Papa's punctuality; no age joke.

In chapter 5 bubbles (rule 36): 'phone' | 'फ़ोन' or 'call' | 'कॉल' anywhere in the chapter; 'pump' | 'पंप', 'motor' | 'मोटर', 'generator' | 'जनरेटर'; 'gate lights' before 5.07; 'old folks' or 'old ways' before 5.15 and 5.24.

To you: any word that gives you a gender ('beta' | 'बेटा', 'bhanja' | 'भांजा', 'bhanji' | 'भांजी', 'bachcha' | 'बच्चा', 'bhai', 'champ', 'yaar', 'hero'), and any Hindi that fails rule 66: 'तुम आ गए?', 'थक गए?', 'करोगे?', 'हमारे इंचार्ज', 'खड़े रहो', 'बैठे रहो'.
Brands of any kind: no phone, car, pump or sweet-shop name (rule 3).
address: NANI: 'Amma' | 'अम्मा'; आप and -इए ('Amma, aap baithiye.'). Short whole sentences; he lets her finish and repeats her last two words. She calls him 'छोटे'.
MUMMY: 'Didi' | 'दीदी'; आप, softened with 'na' ('Didi, rakh lijiye na.'). The first person he rings about anything. She calls him 'Chhote' ('Chhote ji' with आप when she is angry).
PAPA: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी'; आप. To guests, 'the family's railway'. Papa's word for him is for the family address table.
MAUSI: 'Badi Didi' | 'बड़ी दीदी' (plain 'Didi' is Mummy); आप. She calls him 'Munna', तुम.
MAUSA JI: 'Bade Jija ji' | 'बड़े जीजा जी'; आप. He calls him 'Chhote', तुम.
TINKU: 'Tinku'; तुम ('Tinku, ek kaam karo,'). To guests 'our youngest' until December, then 'District scorer se miliye!'. She says 'Mama ji' and आप.
MAMI: 'Boss' | 'बॉस', in front of the family and in private; तुम both ways. Her name is never said on screen; she calls him no name, and 'your Mama ji' to the young ones.
MASTERJI: 'Masterji' | 'मास्टरजी'; आप. CAPTAIN SAHAB: 'Captain sahab' | 'कप्तान साहब'; आप (he greets him 'Catch?').
VENDORS he knows: first name with 'bhai' ('[name] bhai'), आप and -इए ('Ek kaam kijiye'); strangers and guests: 'Bhai sahab', 'Behen ji', 'Aaiye'; आप to all, even when cross.

YOU: तुम, only in rule 66 shapes: commands ('Ek kaam karo', 'gate pe raho', 'batao', 'sambhalo'), 'who should' asks ('Gate pe kaun rahe?' | 'गेट पर कौन रहे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('Sab tumhare bharose.', where तुम्हारे agrees with भरोसे). To others he names you by your job with no possessive that could agree with you ('In-charge se miliye!', 'Poora week inke haath mein', never 'हमारे इंचार्ज'); a message to you opens 'In-charge!!'. No family word for you while rulebook Q7 is open. Your replies: 'Mama ji, sorted.' | 'मामा जी, सब सेट है।' with आप.

Rule 66 checker flags on his lines to or around you, each for a native reader to clear: 'पक्का?' and 'अच्छा।' (words that never change, check 3); 'सब तुम्हारे भरोसे।' (भरोसे ends a sentence on -े and agrees with भरोसा); 'कुर्सियाँ भी,' (the particle भी); 'पंप भेज रहा,' (about himself); 'नौकरी लगी?' and 'अम्मा ने दवाई ली?' (they agree with नौकरी and दवाई).
All of these go into the one family address table the India review asks for, signed off by the Hindi-first readers and the South Indian reader (rule 65).
samples: ORDER, the run-on that grows, to you, ch 5 at Nani's gate, outside any decision beat (commands only, rule 66). EN: 'Do one thing, take the gate, oh, and, / get Bade Jija ji, the chairs too, / everyone in, room for everyone. Sure?' | HINGLISH: 'Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, aur haan, / Bade Jija ji ko bulao, chairs bhi, / sabko andar lo, sabko jagah. Pakka?' | HI: 'एक काम करो, गेट पर रहो, और हाँ, / बड़े जीजा जी को बुलाओ, कुर्सियाँ भी, / सबको अंदर लो, सबको जगह। पक्का?'

WORRYING, to Mummy by phone from the city (the opening, or the writers' ear); the stack waits only for the last answer. EN: 'Didi! Just checking in, oh, and, / Amma's blood pressure? Medicines? Someone with her? Sure?' | HINGLISH: 'Didi! Just checking, kuch nahi, aur haan, / Amma ka BP? Dawai? Koi saath hai? Pakka?' | HI: 'दीदी! ऐसे ही फ़ोन किया, और हाँ, / अम्मा का बीपी? दवाई? कोई साथ है? पक्का?'

LOVE, OUT LOUD, to Nani at the blue gate in December, her palm on his bowed head, his arms round her after (short whole sentences: she is the one he slows for). EN: 'Amma, I missed you. Every day.' | HINGLISH: 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' | HI: 'अम्मा, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगा। रोज़।'

SORRY, blame made bigger, to Mummy, when his night-before booking has Papa at the station at dawn again. EN: 'Didi, it's all my fault. All of it!' | HINGLISH: 'Didi, full kasoor mera. Full!' | HI: 'दीदी, पूरा क़सूर मेरा। पूरा!'

THANKS, credit by job, to the guests at the gate about you (guests off the panel, outside any decision beat; no possessive that could agree with you). EN: 'Meet the in-charge! / The whole week's in their hands, oh, and,' | HINGLISH: 'In-charge se miliye! / Poora week inke haath mein, aur haan,' | HI: 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए! / पूरा हफ़्ता इनके हाथ में, और हाँ,'
THANKS, credit by job, to the same guests about Papa, who met their train. EN: 'Meet the family's railway!' | HINGLISH: 'Ghar ki railway se miliye!' | HI: 'घर की रेलवे से मिलिए!'

PRAISE, made bigger in words, to Tinku in December when the scorers' course letter comes (the writers' ear; on screen it is a message, since Tinku speaks only in ch 4). EN: 'District? Oho! Next the state, then the country, oh, and,' | HINGLISH: 'District? Oho! Ab state, phir poora desh, aur haan,' | HI: 'डिस्ट्रिक्ट? ओहो! अब स्टेट, फिर पूरा देश, और हाँ,'

TO A VENDOR, November, by phone from an auto between sites (the writers' ear for his competence: people first, then 'Achha,' and the job). EN: '[Name] bhai! All well at home? Your mother's knee? / The children's exams? Good. Now, one small job,' | HINGLISH: '[Name] bhai! Ghar mein sab theek? Maa ji ka ghutna? / Bachchon ke exam? Achha. Ab ek kaam kijiye,' | HI: '[नाम] भाई! घर में सब ठीक? माँ जी का घुटना? / बच्चों के इम्तिहान? अच्छा। अब एक काम कीजिए,'

CROSS, to the tent man, November, by phone (the writers' ear, never a twin lead-in): the run-on stops dead, one chop of the free hand on each word, never a shout. EN: '[Name] bhai, "just leaving" yesterday, the day before too, / Today. Now. Here.' | HINGLISH: '[Name] bhai, kal bhi "nikal raha hoon", parson bhi, / Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.' | HI: '[नाम] भाई, कल भी "निकल रहा हूँ", परसों भी, / आज। अभी। यहीं।'

COMFORT, to Nani in the front row, December (short whole sentences). EN: 'Amma, today you just sit. The rest is ours.' | HINGLISH: 'Amma, aaj aap sirf baithiye. Baaki hamare zimme.' | HI: 'अम्मा, आज आप सिर्फ़ बैठिए। बाक़ी हमारे ज़िम्मे।'

LOVE, OUT LOUD, to Mami on the Friday night of the wedding week, in private (the writers' ear only, since her tired beat stays wordless on screen). EN: 'Boss, close the list, morning will do, oh, and, / you held the whole house today. I saw.' | HINGLISH: 'Boss, list band karo, kal subah, aur haan, / aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha.' | HI: 'बॉस, लिस्ट बंद करो, कल सुबह, और हाँ, / आज पूरा घर तुमने सँभाला। मैंने देखा।'

FEAR, to Mami on the balcony the night of the fall (the writers' ear only, since he does not speak in ch 2): the one time his run-on has nowhere to go. EN: 'I wasn't there, Boss. Again.' | HINGLISH: 'Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.' | HI: 'मैं वहाँ नहीं था, बॉस। फिर से।'

A JOKE AT HIMSELF, big and kind (waits on rulebook Q5; opening or album only, never a lead-in or a question bubble, rule 37). EN: 'Plans are Boss's department, / mine's just people, oh, and,' | HINGLISH: 'Plan Boss ka department hai, / mera department sirf log, aur haan,' | HI: 'प्लान बॉस का डिपार्टमेंट है, / मेरा डिपार्टमेंट सिर्फ़ लोग, और हाँ,'

A JOKE ABOUT THE CROWD, with the ten extra chairs he has stacked by the gate (waits on Q5; no figure, the plus-ten stays in his open hand). EN: 'If chairs run short, folk stand, dinner ends sooner,' | HINGLISH: 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega,' | HI: 'कुर्सियाँ कम पड़ीं तो लोग खड़े-खड़े, खाना जल्दी निपटेगा,'

TEASING, to Papa in the opening ('Oho!' where the old file had 'Kamaal!', now Papa's). EN: 'Oho! Jija ji, next year's tickets booked already? / Oh, and mine too, a waiting list will do,' | HINGLISH: 'Oho! habits: Device: a big plain black phone in a thick black rubber case with one corner cracked on a site, painted with the screen dark and no logo, every word live text laid on top (rule 30). In chapter 5 it stays in his trouser pocket: never painted, never typed on screen.
Script: English and Roman Hinglish, never Devanagari (Nani's voice-typed Devanagari is the contrast). In the game's Hindi mode his messages show in Devanagari and keep his bursts and marks.
Shape: the run-on typed as a burst. Four or five short messages, each one clause of it, 'aur haan' a message of its own, then 'calling' before you can reply.

The first message is the person's name, capitalised, with his doubled mark ('Didi!!', 'Jija ji!!', 'In-charge!!'); everything after it is lowercase, kin names included ('amma', 'nani', 'chhote'), with no full stops. To Mami in private the name comes with no mark at all ('Boss').
Marks: '!!' is his; a worry question takes one '?', because '??' is Mausi's; never '!!!'.

Numbers: his bigness is typed in words (sab, everyone, extra, full), never as figures and never as the plus-ten. A digit appears only when a fact someone must act on cannot be said another way, and then he would rather ring.

Emoji: 🎉 for good news, ‼️ for worry, and 🤗 (a face with no person, gender or skin tone) for love typed in words ('miss you all 🤗'): he is the only one in the family who types love. 💯 is retired: it was a number sign and his old number habit. Never a person emoji; no folded hands until the owner rules (realism notes).
Capitals once a year, for joy (Tinku's course letter), never in anger: all caps reads as shouting, the 'aggro uncle' trap (realism notes).

Voice notes from the back of an auto between sites, starting mid-word because he presses record late; shown as a voice-note strip with their words as live text, and they run on like his speech ('...aur haan, aur ek,').

Forwards: only weather warnings for Nani's district, each with one line of his own ('amma ko andar rakhiye na!!'), the warning painted blank. Never politics, religion, gods, famous faces or false news (rule 3; caricature traps).

When: just before his eight o'clock call to Nani, at red lights, and late at night after Mami's list. He replies in seconds or not at all, because he rings instead, and never reads a long message to the end ('ok ok call me').
Short forms: 'pls', 'ok ok', 'msg'. No spelled accent and no typo played for laughs. No English verb with kar ('call karo' became 'call me'), since that frame is Mummy's.
In private with Mami, and only there, his asks come down, in words: 'sabko?' becomes 'ok sab nahi' becomes 'tumhari list'.
The game has no group chat (owner, 23 Oct). On screen he is single messages on a painted blank phone or a message card under a panel, and a message on the player's own phone waits on rulebook Q9.

changed: NUMBERS (C1): every spoken figure struck except the two marked beats, 5.03 '60? 70 kar do!' and 5.27 '60 plates. Pakka.'. The plus-ten stays only as the flashed open hand. His bigness moves into words (aur, sab, sabko, extra, full). The joke '60 kursiyaan? 10 log khade-khade.' became 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega,'; the temper line's 'do din se' became 'kal bhi... parson bhi'.

NUMBERS IN TYPING (C1, typing pass): '2 tickets 14th night' to Papa became 'tomorrow night / me and Boss'; 'tent coming 4 pm' to you became 'tent aaj shaam'; the private 'boss 70 final? / ok 65 / ok ok 60' to Mami became 'sabko bulayein? / ok sab nahi / ok ok tumhari list', so his asks still come down in private, now in words and towards her list; 💯 retired, because it was a number sign.
'KAMAAL!' STRUCK from the Papa tease, now 'Oho!' (matrix 2.15: 'Kamaal hai.' is Papa's new exclamation). 'Oho!' stays his one exclamation, secular, a sound with no word in it.

LOVE LINE (C16): Hinglish 'Amma, I missed you. Bahut.' became 'Roz.', English 'So much.' became 'Every day.', so 'bahut yaad' stays Mausi's alone; his Hindi 'आपके बिना मन नहीं लगा।' already differed and gains 'रोज़।'. Love is now said out loud to more than Nani: 'Didi, I'll miss you.' at a parting, and what Mami did said back to her in private.

SORRY AND THANKS SET (C4: he had neither): sorry is blame made bigger, 'Didi, full kasoor mera. Full!'; thanks is public credit by job, and when he is thanked he gives the credit away ('Not me! Credit Jija ji ka.'). Neither is a deed, and neither uses 'sorry' (Mausi's), 'thank you' (Mami's) or 'shukriya' (yours).

'NO TENSION' STRUCK: Mausi's target gives 'tension' to her English. His reassurance is 'Don't worry' (the realism notes' own example for him, and Mummy's, Papa's and Mausa ji's files already call it his); in Hindi mode 'चिंता मत करो' / 'चिंता नहीं', never फ़िक्र, which is Masterji's.

THE RUN-ON MADE VISIBLE (C2): every bubble but the last ends on a comma, 'aur haan' gets a fixed English form ('oh, and'), and each test line shows the trailing comma inside its one bubble, so his long shape survives the 10-word cap (rule 62) and reads apart from Papa's full stops, Masterji's wander and Mausi's triple.

ENGLISH VERB + KAR STRUCK: 'ok ok call karo' became 'ok ok call me'; the never list now bars 'check karo', 'confirm karo', 'book karo', because the matrix gives that frame to Mummy alone. His English comes as whole clauses, which is what keeps his mix apart from Mummy's.

MIX SPLIT FROM MAMI (C12 near-miss): both switch whole clauses, so the order and the cargo now differ: his English leads and carries jobs and warmth, then Hindi lands on family; hers is a Hindi clause, then an English status.

HINDI MODE KEPT SORTABLE: he keeps more English loan words in Devanagari than anyone (एक्स्ट्रा, फ़ुल, सेट, नो प्रॉब्लम, क्रेडिट, डिपार्टमेंट), because the blind test runs again in Hindi and a voice that sorts only in Hinglish fails two of three modes.
ENGLISH MODE: 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job', so his one Indian-English turn stays one turn.

TEA TAKEN OUT OF HIS CARE (C3: tea carried four people's care): 'Boss, chai. List kal.' became 'Boss, list band karo, kal subah, aur haan,' / 'aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha.', love said in words, and the old clipped two-word shape (C2) gone; at the gate 'sabko chai' became 'sabko jagah'.
JOKE AT HIMSELF ADDED: 'Plan Boss ka department hai,' / 'mera department sirf log, aur haan,'. The target asks for humour big, kind and at himself, and the old jokes were about the crowd.

POLITE FORMS FIXED: 'In-charge se milo!' became 'miliye!' (guests are elders and strangers); vendors get 'Ek kaam kijiye' to match his own address rule, 'आप to all'; forwards to Didi say 'rakhiye na', the आप softened with 'na' that his address rule for her asks.
'POORI GALI' NOT USED: Nani's new voice owns 'मेरी पूरी गली।', so his lane is 'gali mein sabko'.

TYPING MARKS: the opener is the listener's name with '!!' and the rest lowercase, one consistent rule where the old samples mixed cases; 'DISTRICT LEVEL!!!' became '!!' (doubled is his mark, triples are Mausi's shape); 'r u at nani's' (whose Hindi 'यहाँ हो' trips the rule 66 checker) is gone; love is now typed in words with 🤗, the one family member who types it.

OWNERSHIP GUARDS ADDED to the never list: 'Pehle ___' (yours), any 'arre' (Captain sahab's), 'first class' and every ordinal, 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' (Mausa ji's), 'Badhaai ho' beside 'Main hoon na' as famous titles, and 'Thank God' and its kin named outright, since a city man reaches for them first.

C10 FIXED FOR HIM: asked how he is, he answers 'Full fit!' and turns straight to everyone else's medicines, with no figure and no trade dodge, which keeps his want (worried about everyone but himself) on the page.
C15: in the test set he speaks to the tent man, Papa, Mummy, a neighbour and a child, not only to you, so he is heard with the others.

KEPT, unchanged in substance: his essence, want, fear and contradiction (worries about everything, plans nothing; makes anyone come); 'Pakka?' and its turn at 5.27; 'Ek kaam karo'; the stacked worry questions he never answers himself; people before business; the cross tell (the run-on breaking into single words with a chop of the hand); slowing down only for Nani; fear said only to Mami; the address table.

OPEN, for the owner and readers: keep both marked figures (5.03 and 5.27)? A Hindi-first reader checks 'घर की रेलवे' (the gender of रेलवे), 'फ़ुल फ़िट', 'नो प्रॉब्लम' and 'क्रेडिट' in Hindi mode, and 'Kursiyaan kam padin'; 🤗 is proposed as his and no other file claims it; every joke still waits on rulebook Q5.
